performers: Orchestra and Choir of Teatro Reale dell’Opera di Roma (current Commons attribution; disputed)
intro: Four orchestral blows tear open Verdi’s vision of judgement. In this opening number of the Dies irae, the chorus passes from a full-throated cry to a frightened murmur.

sections.label: A · Four blows and a cry
sections.mNote: Rushing strings carry the chorus’s cry of judgement

sections.label: A′ · The chorus begins to murmur
sections.mNote: Single choral parts repeat Dies irae above quiet strings

sections.label: B · Trembling voices
sections.mNote: Repeated syllables, plucked bass notes and little upward string runs

cues.title: Four blows in G minor
cues.text: Four separated G minor chords precede the rushing strings and the chorus’s cry: “Dies irae” — “Day of wrath.” Verdi writes Allegro agitato. The bass drum’s blows cut across the beat; the orchestral runs leave the singers scarcely room to breathe.
cues.evidence: Verdi, Requiem, Eulenburg full score, plate E.E.4864, pp. 21–24, opening of No. 2. Latin words from the medieval Requiem sequence; translation ours. Score: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/71/IMSLP407348-PMLP01812-Verdi_Requiem_whole.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A memorial in Milan
cues.text: At the church of San Marco in Milan, on 22 May 1874, Verdi conducts his Requiem for the writer Alessandro Manzoni. It is the first anniversary of Manzoni’s death. Three days later, the same singers take the work to La Scala.
cues.evidence: Teatro dell’Opera di Roma historical archive, premiere details: https://archiviostorico.operaroma.it/concerto/messa-da-requiem/. The subsequent La Scala performance is documented in the performance history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Verdi).

cues.title: A Requiem for Rossini first
cues.text: After Rossini’s death in 1868, Verdi proposes a Requiem shared among Italian composers and writes its last number, the Libera me. The performance, planned for 13 November 1869, never takes place. In 1871 he tells an admirer: “There are so many, many Masses for the Dead.”
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner’s programme note: Verdi’s contribution to the joint Rossini Requiem was the Libera me, the work was not performed as planned, and in 1871 he wrote to an admirer, “There are so many, many Masses for the Dead. It would be pointless to add one more.” https://geraldlarner.com/work/verdi-messa-da-requiem . BR-Klassik (Bayerischer Rundfunk, Susanna Felix, 2017): the Requiem was to be given in Bologna on 13 November 1869, the first anniversary of Rossini’s death; the score was finished in time and the performance did not happen: https://www.br-klassik.de/themen/klassik-entdecken/messa-per-rossini-verdi-urauffuehrung-platzt-was-heute-geschah-1869-100.html

cues.title: The choir fears its words
cues.text: “Quantus tremor est futurus” — “How great the trembling will be.” The chorus repeats its notes softly, marked sotto voce. Violins and cellos send little runs back and forth above plucked bass notes. The people announcing the judgement now sound terrified of it.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 39–42, Quantus tremor: choral pp and sotto voce, viola and bass pizzicato, alternating violin and cello figures. Latin sequence, translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The cry breaks into murmurs
transitions.from: A · Four blows and a cry
transitions.to: A′ · The chorus begins to murmur
transitions.how: The bass holds G as the orchestral chords diminish. The brass fall silent; clarinet and bassoon keep their winding little scales. Separate choral parts repeat “Dies irae”, marked pp cupo — darkly — above the strings. The same words pass from the whole crowd to small, exposed groups.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 36–38: sustained G bass, diminuendo, and separate choral entries marked Soli and pp cupo.

transitions.title: A stammer over plucked strings
transitions.from: A′ · The chorus begins to murmur
transitions.how: Violas and basses pluck their notes while the violins and cellos alternate short upward runs. Low brass sustain beneath the clipped woodwind chords. The chorus enters pp sotto voce on “Quantus tremor”: repeated syllables over an accompaniment that never quite keeps still.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg full score, pp. 39–42, orchestral preparation and Quantus tremor entry.

source.title: Verdi, Requiem — Eulenburg full score, plate E.E.4864
source.locator: PDF pages 21–42, opening Dies irae number. “Tuba” represents the score’s ophicleide/bass-brass staff, not a verified instrument used in this transfer. No solo singers occur in this number; the offstage trumpets belong to the following Tuba mirum.

timeline.note: Four orchestral blows and rushing figures; the chorus enters after the opening attacks.
Choral entry region; lower and upper voices enter in succession, not as one instantaneous block.
Expanded opening declamation, including bass-drum punctuation in the written score.
Diminishing region with progressively reduced scoring; not every group sounds continuously.
Quiet Quantus tremor region: repeated choral notes, active strings and restrained wind support.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: He could make a catchy tenor tune sound like a death sentence simply by letting the wrong man hear it.
facts: Provesi in Busseto; private lessons with Lavigna after Milan’s Conservatoire rejected him
Milan · Venice · Florence · Rome · Naples · Paris · St Petersburg · Cairo
Piave, Cammarano and Boito were his principal collaborators
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred music, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Milan’s Conservatoire turned Giuseppe Verdi down in 1832. Antonio Barezzi, a merchant from Busseto who had helped pay for his move to Milan, kept supporting him, and Verdi studied privately with Vincenzo Lavigna, formerly a musician at La Scala. He learnt counterpoint and went to the theatre. Four years later he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took a municipal musical post in Busseto. His patrons were people who had heard him play, watched him grow up and put their own money behind him.

His parents kept an inn and shop at Le Roncole, where he was born in 1813. He learnt the organ locally, then studied with Ferdinando Provesi in nearby Busseto. Oberto, his first opera, reached La Scala in 1839 and earned him further commissions. His daughter Virginia had died in 1838; his son Icilio died in 1839, and Margherita in June 1840. That September the theatre presented his comedy Un giorno di regno. It failed. Verdi was twenty-six and had lost his wife and both children.
